title: Penalties are graduated for Aligned Delegates but mandatory derecognition for anything resembling a Governance Attack
content:
A.1.5.9.2 gives the Core Facilitator authority to "impose an appropriate penalty up to and including derecognition," then splits that discretion in two. A.1.5.9.2.1 sends Aligned Delegate breaches of AC requirements to the Graduated Response Framework at A.1.6.6.1. A.1.5.9.2.2 removes discretion entirely at the top end: "In cases where severe actions or violations occur that can be reasonably interpreted as Governance Attacks, the Alignment Conserver must be promptly derecognized."

The threshold wording deserves attention. It is not "where a Governance Attack has occurred" but where actions "can be reasonably interpreted as" one — an interpretive trigger, deliberately set below proof. Combined with the 51% standard, this means the severe tier fires on a reading of the conduct rather than a demonstration of intent.

What distinguishes that tier is spelled out at A.1.5.9.2.2.0.3.1: a governance attack "is reserved for misaligned acts with the near-term potential to severely compromise the Ecosystem's foundational structure and operational integrity," and "in contrast to mild breaches, which may involve actors with unintentional or benign motivations, a Governance Attack is distinguished by its deliberate and premeditated nature. Actors orchestrating such attacks are likely driven by strategic intent." So the dividing line is **intent plus systemic reach**, not magnitude of damage alone.

The two-tier design is the sensible resolution of a genuine tension in the AC regime. A single mandatory-derecognition rule for all breaches would be brittle and would burn competent delegates on technicalities; unlimited discretion at the top would let a facilitator soften a response to an actual attack. Graduating the ordinary cases and hard-coding the extreme one gets proportionality where it is affordable and certainty where it is not.

NR-7 concedes the boundary is undefined, asking what qualifies as "severe" and what "specifically constitute[s] a 'Governance Attack'," including "criteria or frameworks for assessing intent." The tier that removes all discretion is the one whose entry condition is least specified.
description: A.1.5.9.2.1 routes AD breaches to a Graduated Response Framework, while A.1.5.9.2.2 removes all discretion where actions can reasonably be interpreted as Governance Attacks.
